'''James Edward Young''' (born January 18, 1926) is an American physicist who was the first black tenured faculty member in the Department of Physics at [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]]. He was a founding member of the [[National Society of Black Physicists]] and a mentor for [[Shirley Ann Jackson]].

== Early life and education ==
Young was born in [[Wheeling, West Virginia]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://www.nsbp.org/nsbp-news/bhm-physics-profiles/2018-honorees/105-james-young|title=James Young|website=www.nsbp.org|access-date=2019-09-18}}</ref> He attended Lincoln High School, a [[segregated school]] for African-American children of [[Ohio County, West Virginia]] and [[Marshall County, West Virginia]],<ref>[https://www.ohiocountylibrary.org/wheeling-history/4070   Lincoln School]. Ohio Public Library.</ref> and graduated in 1941.<ref name=":0" />

Young studied physics at [[Howard University]], and earned his bachelor's degree in 1946.<ref name=YoungMITPhysD>[https://physics.mit.edu/faculty/james-young/  James Edward Young. Professor of Physics, Emeritus.] MIT Department of Physics.</ref> From 1946 to 1949, he was a physics instructor at the [[Hampton Institute]], while working on a master's degree in physics at Howard.<ref name=YoungMITPhysD/>

In 1949, he joined [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] as a research assistant.<ref name=YoungMITPhysD/> In 1953, he earned a Ph.D. in physics, and his MIT dissertation was titled, “Propagation of Sound In Attenuating Ducts Containing Absorptive Strips.”<ref name=YoungMITPhysD/> He completed a one-year Post-doctoral Fellow in Acoustics at MIT in 1954.<ref name=YoungMITPhysD/>

Young's early research considered the propagation of noise in pipes.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Young|first1=J. E.|last2=Mawardi|first2=O. K.|date=1954-09-01|title=On the Propagation of Noise in Pipes. II|journal=The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America|volume=26|issue=5|pages=938|doi=10.1121/1.1927969|issn=0001-4966|bibcode=1954ASAJ...26..938Y|doi-access=free}}</ref> He was a member of [[Sigma Pi Sigma]], [[Sigma Xi]], and [[Beta Kappa Chi]].<ref name="History">{{Cite web|url=http://mitblackhistory.blogspot.com/2015/10/pioneering-physicist-james-edward-young.html|title=Capture the MO*MIT: MIT Physicist - James Edward Young|last=History|first=Mit Black|date=2015-10-24|website=Capture the MO*MIT|access-date=2019-09-18}}</ref> After earning his PhD, Young joined [[Los Alamos National Laboratory]], where he began working on particle physics. He investigated [[pion]]s<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Das|first1=T.|last2=Guralnik|first2=G. S.|last3=Mathur|first3=V. S.|last4=Low|first4=F. E.|last5=Young|first5=J. E.|date=1967-05-01|title=Electromagnetic Mass Difference of Pions|journal=Physical Review Letters|volume=18|issue=18|pages=759–761|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.18.759|bibcode=1967PhRvL..18..759D}}</ref> and [[Deuterium|deuteron]] stripping theory.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Young|first=James E.|date=1961-02-01|title=The optical model and deuteron stripping|journal=Nuclear Physics|volume=23|pages=40–52|doi=10.1016/0029-5582(61)90237-1|issn=0029-5582|bibcode=1961NucPh..23...40Y}}</ref>

== Research and career ==
Young researched and taught theoretical particle physics, [[critical phenomena]], and nuclear physics in the [[MIT Center for Theoretical Physics]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Chang|first1=T. S.|last2=Nicoll|first2=J. F.|last3=Young|first3=J. E.|date=1978-08-21|title=A closed-form differential renormalization-group generator for critical dynamics|journal=Physics Letters A|volume=67|issue=4|pages=287–290|doi=10.1016/0375-9601(78)90306-7|issn=0375-9601|bibcode=1978PhLA...67..287C}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.blackhistory.mit.edunode/122|title=James E. Young, 1983|website=MIT Black History|language=en|access-date=2019-12-30}}{{Dead link|date=September 2024 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> He earned tenure in the Department of Physics at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] in 1969, and was the first black member of faculty to do so.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.blackhistory.mit.edunode/122|title=James E. Young, 1983|website=MIT Black History|language=en|access-date=2019-09-18}}{{Dead link|date=September 2024 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> He was interested in the intermediate structures in nuclear reactions.<ref name=":1">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=5t8eBgAAQBAJ&q=James+Edward+Young+many+body+scattering&pg=PA129|title=Intermediate Structure in Nuclear Reactions|last1=Kennedy|first1=Hugh P.|last2=Schrils|first2=Rudolph|date=2015-01-13|publisher=University Press of Kentucky|isbn=9780813163314|language=en}}</ref> He contributed to several textbooks, including ''Nuclear, Particle and Many Body Physics''<ref>{{Citation|last1=Jones|first1=C. EDWARD|chapter=Generalized O(2,1) Expansion for Asymptotically Growing Amplitudes**This work is supported in part by the U. S. Atomic Energy Commission under Contract AT(30-1)-2098.|date=1972-01-01|chapter-url=http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B9780125082013500272|title=Nuclear, Particle and Many Body Physics|pages=476–496|editor-last=Morse|editor-first=PHILIP M.|publisher=Academic Press|isbn=9780125082013|access-date=2019-09-18|last2=Low|first2=F. E.|last3=Young|first3=J. E.|editor2-last=Feld|editor2-first=BERNARD T.|editor3-last=Feshbach|editor3-first=HERMAN|editor4-last=Wilson|editor4-first=RICHARD}}</ref> and the ''Intermediate Structure in Nuclear Reactions.<ref name=":1" />'' Young was the doctoral advisor for [[Shirley Ann Jackson]], the first African-American woman to earn a PhD at [[MIT]], as well as [[Sylvester James Gates]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nsbp.org/nsbp-news/bhm-physics-profiles/2017-honorees/31-shirley-jackson|title=Shirley Jackson|website=www.nsbp.org|access-date=2019-09-18}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_7WSzRAU_rUC&q=Jim+Young+MIT+particle+physics&pg=PA122|title=Sisters in Science: Conversations with Black Women Scientists about Race, Gender, and Their Passion for Science|last=Jordan|first=Diann|date=2006|publisher=Purdue University Press|isbn=9781557534453|location=|pages=|language=en}}</ref>

In 1977, Young was a founding member of the [[National Society of Black Physicists]].<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://web.mit.edu/physics/people/faculty/young_james.html|title=MIT Department of Physics|website=web.mit.edu|access-date=2019-09-18}}</ref><ref name="World Scientific">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=htDUCgAAQBAJ&q=James+Young+national+society+black&pg=PA109|title=Edward Bouchet: The First African-american Doctorate|last=E|first=Mickens Ronald|date=2002-02-04|publisher=World Scientific|isbn=9789814488884|language=en}}</ref> He founded the society with [[Ronald E. Mickens]], with whom he had previously discussed senior Black physicists who became role models for their students. They hosted a meeting at [[Fisk University]] to celebrate these "elders", including [[Halson V. Eagleson]], [[Donald Anderson Edwards|Donald Edwards]], and [[John McNeile Hunter]]. The National Society of Black Physicists emerged from these meetings, an independent society led by African-Americans who "created and developed activities and programs for themselves".<ref name="World Scientific"/>

In 2025, Young is recognized as Professor of Physics, ''Emeritus'', at MIT.<ref name=YoungMITPhysD/>

== Personal life ==
Young married E. Elaine Hunter, with whom he has one child, James E. Young III.<ref name="History"/>
